Antoni Gaudí. The Catalan architect whose organic, sculptural approach created fantastical buildings that seemed to grow rather than stand.

Gaudí was born in 1852 and died in 1926. His most famous work is the Sagrada Família basilica in Barcelona, which he began designing in 1883 and worked on until his death in 1926. It blends Gothic and organic forms with towering spires and intricate stone carving that has become Barcelona's icon. He also created Park Güell between 1900 and 1914, a terraced garden suburb with undulating benches, colorful ceramic mosaics, and organic architectural forms nestled into a Catalan hillside.

Gaudí pioneered the use of trencadís, a mosaic technique using broken ceramic tiles and salvaged materials, creating richly patterned, colorful surfaces throughout his work. He designed Casa Batlló and Casa Milà in Barcelona, apartment buildings with rippling, bone-like stone facades and undulating balconies that blur the line between architecture and sculpture. His rejection of Cartesian geometry and straight lines led him to use parabolic arches, hyperbolic surfaces, and forms derived from nature—bones, shells, and plants. He studied the structural properties of catenary curves, the natural form of hanging cables, and applied them inverted as load-bearing elements in his buildings.

His late work became increasingly religious, and he lived in virtual solitude at the Sagrada Família, perfecting its construction. He shares a philosophical approach to organic architecture with Frank Lloyd Wright, another contemporary pursuing organic design through a different cultural lens, though both rejected rigid modernism. Gaudí was the central figure in Catalan Modernisme, a movement parallel to Art Nouveau that influenced design across Europe.
